claims.text: As-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 is a single-phase refractory multicomponent alloy.
As-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
As-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
The reported 13.5% terminal strain of HfZrTiTa0.53 represents limited tensile ductility.
A 600–700 °C anneal is below the recrystallization temperature of HfZrTiTa0.53.
Annealing for 10–30 minutes at 600–700 °C will induce secondary-phase precipitation in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The anneal will produce approximately 1–3 wt% of a ductile secondary phase localized at grain boundaries or triple junctions.
The grain-boundary secondary phase will impede crack initiation at stress-concentration sites.
The grain-boundary secondary phase will promote a more homogeneous tensile strain distribution.
Restricting the secondary phase to a small fraction will preserve the strength of the primary matrix.
Restricting the secondary phase to a small fraction will preserve impact-triggered chemical energy release.
The anneal will increase uniform tensile elongation by at least approximately 5 percentage points, from about 13.5% to near 18%.
The annealed alloy will retain yield strength within ±5% of 786 MPa.
The annealed alloy will retain compressive strength within ±10% of 1314 MPa.
The annealed HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy will have impact-triggered chemical energy release comparable to tungsten-alloy fragments.
The predicted mechanical benefits apply at room temperature under quasi-static tensile and compressive loading near 10^-3 s^-1.
The predicted mechanical benefits may remain applicable at temperatures up to approximately 600 °C.
The treatment can preserve high strength while improving tensile elongation in a multicomponent alloy.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% value is described as terminal tensile strain but is then used as though it were the baseline uniform tensile elongation; terminal strain and uniform elongation are distinct measurements.

The falsification design appears to place impact tests under quasi-static loading at approximately 10^-3 s^-1, whereas the boundary separately invokes standard impact conditions; an impact test is not quasi-static at that strain rate.

The predicted impact outcome is defined relative to tungsten-alloy fragments, while the falsification rule tests only for a reduction relative to the untreated HfZrTiTa0.53 control. These comparators are not equivalent unless the control is first shown to match the tungsten-alloy benchmark.
